title: Hereditary Macular Dystrophies: Best Disease vs. Stargardt Disease
summary: A comprehensive clinical comparison between the two most common inherited macular dystrophies. This guide covers the genetic, electrophysiological, and multimodal imaging hallmarks essential for board certification and clinical practice.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: Stargardt Disease (STGD1) is the most common autosomal recessive macular dystrophy, characterized by subretinal lipofuscin accumulation and progressive RPE atrophy. Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene, leading to the accumulation of yellowish lipofuscin-like material (egg-yolk lesion) in the sub-retinal space.

sections.title: The 5 Stages of Best Disease (BVMD)
content: Stage 1: Pre-vitelliform - Normal fundus; Abnormal EOG (Arden Ratio < 1.55).
Stage 2: Vitelliform - Classic 'Egg-Yolk' lesion (3-5mm) in the macula.
Stage 3: Pseudohypopyon - Partial resorption of yellowish material; fluid-level appears.
Stage 4: Vitelliruptive - 'Scrambled Egg' appearance; material breaks up, vision drops.
Stage 5: Atrophic/Cicatricial - RPE atrophy or fibrous scarring; potential CNV development.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Ocular Signs
content: STGD: 'Pisciform' flecks (fish-tail shaped) at the level of RPE.
STGD: Bull's eye maculopathy or beaten-bronze appearance.
STGD: Peripapillary sparing (highly characteristic).
BVMD: Solitary, well-circumscribed yellow subfoveal lesion.
BVMD: Usually bilateral, though can be asymmetric.
BVMD: Retinal periphery is typically normal.

branches: FFA: 'Dark Choroid' in 80% of STGD (blocked background fluorescence)
FAF: Hyper-autofluorescent flecks in STGD; Intense Hyper-AF in Vitelliform stage of BVMD
OCT: STGD - Loss of EZ zone, RPE thinning; BVMD - Subretinal hyper-reflective material
OCT-A: Monitoring for Type 2 CNV in late stages of both diseases

sections.title: STGD Classification (Fishman)
content: Stage 1: Pigmentary changes in fovea, no flecks within 1DD.
Stage 2: Flecks beyond 1DD, may extend to arcades.
Stage 3: Diffuse flecks, resorbing flecks with RPE atrophy.
Stage 4: Diffuse RPE atrophy; extensive choriocapillaris loss.

sections.title: Red Flags: Potential Complications
content: Sudden metamorphopsia (sign of CNV)
Subretinal hemorrhage in BVMD Stage 5
Rapidly progressive vision loss in STGD1
High sensitivity to Vitamin A in Stargardt

rows: Smaller lesion, Normal EOG, onset > 40 years
History of Hydroxychloroquine or Thioridazine use
Profound early photophobia, severely abnormal ERG early
Variant of STGD1; flecks without early macular atrophy

sections.title: Clinical Management & Protocol
content: Step 1: Genetic Counseling and Testing (ABCA4/BEST1).
Step 2: Low vision assessment and tinted lenses (UV protection).
Step 3: STGD Avoidance: Stop Vitamin A supplements (accelerates A2E).
Step 4: CNV Surveillance: Amsler grid and periodic OCT-A.
Step 5: Treatment of CNV: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept).

content.explanation: BEST disease involves the BEST1 gene, chromosome 11, and usually starts with 1 central lesion. EOG is the #1 diagnostic electrophysiology test.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: ProgStar Study: Longitudinal data on STGD progression using FAF and microperimetry.
TEGSET Clinical Trial: Exploring gene therapy (lentiviral vectors) for ABCA4 replacement.
Emixustat: A visual cycle modulator aimed at reducing A2E accumulation in Stargardt (Phase 3).
ALKEUS Study (Gildeuretinpa): Deuterated Vitamin A to slow lipofuscin formation.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 'Dark Choroid' on FFA is diagnostic for Stargardt but absent in 20% of cases.
Best disease patients often maintain surprisingly good vision despite the 'Egg-yolk' appearance.
If EOG is normal, it is NOT Best disease.
UV-blocking sunglasses are mandatory for all Stargardt patients.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Best disease may be found incidentally during school screenings.
Stargardt may present as 'oculocutaneous albinism' mimic due to foveal hypoplasia-like appearance.
Psychosocial support and IEP (Individualized Education Program) are vital for school-age children.
